blocks.value: There are two ways to create a String: assign a string literal directly, or use the new keyword with the String constructor.

String strGreeting = "Hello World!";      // string literal
String strName = "Jess Diaz";              // string literal
String strGreeting2 = new String("Hello World!"); // using new

This distinction matters for comparison: string literals with the same content share one memory location, but strings created with new always get their own separate memory location, even if the content is identical.

Use == to check whether two variables point to the same object in memory; use .equals() to check whether their content is the same. For strings, always use .equals() unless you specifically need to check object identity.

Strings are also immutable. Once created, a String's content can never change. Unlike a primitive variable (where num++ actually changes num's stored value), every String method that seems to "modify" a string actually returns a brand new string instead.
